questions.prompt: An advertisement always ends by asking its reader to do something. Which line of this festival page is the one that asks?

options.text: Get your pass at the North Gate before the first of April.
The pass is valid for ten days from the day it is stamped.
Every pass holder receives a free souvenir on arrival.
The Palm Garden opens at nine every morning of the week.

questions.explanation: An advertisement is not written to be admired: it wants a move out of you, and the last thing it does is name that move — go there, buy it, book before a date. The verb gives it away, because it is the only one on the page aimed straight at the reader with no subject in front of it. The three other lines describe the offer instead: how long it lasts, what comes free with it, when a garden opens. All three are useful, and not one of them asks anything of you. Find the imperative and you have found what the page wants.

questions.prompt: You have just read about a festival package and you want to say that it attracts you. Which sentence uses "sounds interesting" correctly?

options.text: Sounds interesting the group pass you offer.
It sounds interesting of the group pass you offer.
The group pass you offer sounds interesting.
I sound interested in the group pass you offer.

questions.explanation: One frame of the family puts the thing in front, because the thing is the subject of the verb sound: your pass sounds interesting, the exhibition sounds interesting. The four others take it behind — I'm interested in the pass, I'd like to know more about the pass, I'm keen on it. Leave the front of the sentence empty and the verb has no subject at all; and it sounds interesting needs what follows to say what it is, not to hang a preposition on the offer. As for a person who sounds interested, that is somebody heard on the telephone, not a pass in a brochure.

questions.prompt: A festival pass promises "a discount at the craft market". What does the holder get there?

options.text: He takes one object of his own choice without paying.
He may go into the market before the other visitors.
He is given a small present as he leaves the market.
He pays less than the price marked on the object.

questions.explanation: A discount is a reduction: the price on the label comes down, and you still pay what is left of it. The word for paying nothing is free, and a festival that gave its craft market away would print that word in large letters. A discount says nothing either about the hour you may go in or about a present at the door — those are other promises, and they live in other lines of the advertisement. Read the word for exactly what it says: less money, not no money.

questions.prompt: The word "capital" is written with two letters a, and English does not give them the same sound. Which line describes them correctly?

options.text: Both letters a carry the [æ] of "package".
The first a is the [æ] of "package", the last the [ə] of "festival".
The first a is the [ə] of "festival", the last the [æ] of "package".
Both letters a carry the [ə] of "festival".

questions.explanation: English keeps its full vowels for the syllables that carry the stress and lets the others collapse into the weak [ə]. Capital is said CAP-i-tal, so the a of the stressed opening syllable stays the wide-open [æ] heard in package, while the a at the end, with no stress on it, sinks to the [ə] heard at the end of festival. The same letter, in the same word, with two different sounds — which is exactly why you find the stress before you decide the vowel, and never the other way round.

questions.prompt: You are writing to a festival office to ask what its group pass includes. Which subject line does its job?

options.text: Travel
Hello, I read your advertisement and I would like to ask you several questions
Group pass — request for information
Please answer me as quickly as you can

questions.explanation: A subject line is a label, not the message and not a shout. In four to six words it must tell a reader who opens ninety messages a day what this one is asking for, and let him find it again a week later. Travel names a whole continent of messages and settles nothing. A first sentence pasted into the box is far too long to be taken in at a glance, and it repeats what the message says anyway. And a line that only presses for a quick reply announces what you want from the reader without ever saying what about.
